question: A 3-year-old child referred for genetic consultation to assess psychomotor retardation, language delay and hyperactivity without significant dysmorphic features or associated malformations. He is the first child of a healthy, young and non-consanguineous couple. A maternal uncle has mental retardation and the maternal grandmother presented early ovarian failure. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be the most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?

options.opa: Genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Psychomotor retardation, language delay, and hyperactivity -> Neurodevelopmental disorder -> Genetic consultation for diagnostic evaluation -> 80% CHAIN: Family history of mental retardation and early ovarian failure -> Consider genetic etiology -> Genetic testing for underlying genetic abnormalities -> 75% CHAIN: Absence of dysmorphic features or malformations -> Less likely chromosomal abnormality -> Genetic testing for specific gene mutations -> 70% CHAIN: First child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents -> Low likelihood of inherited metabolic disorder -> Less priority for complete metabolic study -> 80%
enhanced_information: Given the presentation of psychomotor retardation, language delay, and hyperactivity without dysmorphic features or malformations, the most appropriate diagnostic test would be a genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene. This is supported by the family history of mental retardation and early ovarian failure, indicating a potential genetic etiology. The absence of dysmorphic features makes chromosomal abnormalities less likely, reducing the priority for high resolution karyotype. Complete metabolic study is of lower priority due to the low likelihood of an inherited metabolic disorder in this context.
analysis: Given the clinical presentation of psychomotor retardation, language delay, and hyperactivity without dysmorphic features, along with the family history of mental retardation and early ovarian failure, the most appropriate diagnostic test to establish the diagnosis would be a genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene. This aligns with the enhanced information provided and is in line with the suspicion of Fragile X syndrome. High resolution karyotype is less likely to yield the diagnosis in this case due to the absence of dysmorphic features. Complete metabolic study is of lower priority given the clinical presentation and family history.
